title: TNT: Improving Chunkwise Training for Test-Time Memorization
authors: Zeman Li (USC / Google Research), Ali Behrouz, Yuan Deng, Peilin Zhong, Praneeth Kacham, Mahdi Karami, Meisam Razaviyayn, Vahab Mirrokni (Google Research)
tldr: TNT is a two-stage TRAINING paradigm (not a new architecture) for deep test-time-memorization models such as Titans and TTT, designed to break the fixed trade-off imposed by the chunk-size hyperparameter, where large chunks give hardware-efficient training but degrade quality and small chunks give quality but <5-10% FLOPs utilization. Stage 1 pre-trains with a hierarchical memory: one sequential global deep memory running at a huge chunk size (C_G = 2048) for long-range context, plus N parallel local deep memories whose fast-weight states are periodically reset to a shared learnable initial state W_init, which severs the non-linear recurrence across sequence shards and enables massive context parallelism; a Q-K Projection (projecting the query onto the running key-covariance subspace) fixes the domain mismatch between writing with keys and reading with queries. Stage 2 briefly fine-tunes (~5% of pre-training compute) with a smaller local chunk size (ideally C_L' = 1) to cure the newly identified train/inference chunk-size mismatch, aligning the model with prefill (global memory, big chunks) + decode (local memory, chunk 1). On 150M-parameter Titans trained on 10B tokens (TPUv5, JAX, no custom kernels), TNT reaches the target loss up to 17.37x faster than the most accurate Titans baseline (C=8) while IMPROVING average perplexity (23.09 vs 25.07) and beating the vanilla Transformer (23.58); at 32K context a pure-JAX TNT with C_L=128 is even 1.3x faster per step than FlashAttention.
problem_and_motivation:
Deep memory modules -- RNN-like layers whose recurrent state is the weight vector of a small neural network updated by gradient descent on a self-supervised loss at every token (TTT, Titans, Atlas) -- are more expressive than linear memory modules (linear attention, RetNet, GLA, DeltaNet, Mamba-2) because their state transition is non-linear and their state is a deep network rather than a matrix. But they train catastrophically slowly. The reason is chunkwise parallel training: to parallelize the token-serial inner-loop update, the sequence is cut into chunks of size C and all gradients inside a chunk are taken with respect to the chunk-start state. Small chunks (C = 8-64) preserve a fine-grained, 'fresh' learning signal and give the best quality, but produce many small, memory-bound operations that fail to saturate accelerators -- the paper cites FLOPs utilization below 5-10% of peak (quoting Zhang, Bi, et al. 2025 / LaCT). Large chunks saturate hardware but coarsen the inner-loop updates and hurt quality. Linear memory modules escape this with SRAM-resident chunkwise kernels, but those kernels fundamentally rely on LINEAR state transitions and closed-form intra/inter-chunk decompositions; they cannot be applied to a deep memory whose recurrence passes through non-linearities (e.g., LayerNorm between chunks, MLP forward/backward). Parallelizing non-linear recurrences over sequence length is a long-standing open problem (parallel scan does not apply).

The paper crystallizes this into three named challenges. Challenge 1 (efficiency): no efficient training implementation exists for deep memories at small chunk sizes; training is memory-bound, not compute-bound. Challenge 2 (compression/retrieval inconsistency): the inner loop trains f(W, .) to map KEYS to values, but retrieval feeds it a QUERY q_t, an input from a different domain than the one the mapping was fit on -- a train/use domain shift inside the memory itself. Challenge 3 (chunk-size mismatch): quality is sharply sensitive to using the SAME chunk size at inference as at pre-training. Figure 2 (550M Titans pre-trained at C=64) shows validation perplexity as a function of inference chunk size: 36.45 at C=8, 34.15 at 16, 24.23 at 32, 13.78 at 64 (the training chunk size, the optimum), 15.5 at 128, 17.88 at 256, 22.4 at 512. This contradicts the intuition that smaller inference chunks (fresher updates) should always help: the model over-specializes to the training resolution. It also blocks the ideal serving configuration -- decode with chunk size 1 -- because a model pre-trained at a big chunk collapses when run that way. Prior mitigations are judged insufficient: LaCT (Zhang, Bi, et al. 2025) pairs huge chunks with window attention, which circumvents rather than solves the problem, entangles memory with attention, and ignores the need for chunk ~1 at decode; log-linear attention (Guo et al. 2025) is hierarchical but restricted to linear memories. TNT's goal is to decouple training efficiency from inference performance so the bulk of pre-training runs at maximum throughput while the final model is optimal at fine-grained (even chunk-1) inference.

Scaffolding note for inference-side readers: 'chunkwise training' here is about the INNER memorization loop's granularity, not gradient-accumulation or batching; and the perplexity sensitivity in Challenge 3 is an inference-time phenomenon they can directly relate to -- the same checkpoint gives wildly different quality depending on how often you apply the memory update at serving time.
core_mechanism:
BASE ABSTRACTION (Sec. 2.1). A deep memory module maintains fast weights $W$ parameterizing a sub-network $f(W,\cdot):\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ (a small deep net, e.g., a 2-layer MLP), updated online during BOTH training and inference. Each token $x_t$ (a $d$-dim vector) is projected to query/key/value $q_t,k_t,v_t\in\mathbb{R}^d$ by slow-weight projections. Two operations per token:

Memory Compression: $W_t \leftarrow W_{t-1} - \eta_t\, \nabla_W \mathcal{L}\big(f(W_{t-1},k_t),\, v_t\big)$   (Eq. 1)
Memory Retrieval: $o_t = f(W_t, q_t)$   (Eq. 2)

Symbols: $\mathcal{L}(\cdot,\cdot)$ is a self-supervised inner loss (e.g., MSE $\|f(W,k_t)-v_t\|^2$) that writes the association $k_t \mapsto v_t$ into $W$; $\eta_t$ is a LEARNED, data-dependent inner-loop learning rate (a slow-weight function of the token); $o_t$ is the layer output. The recurrence $W_t = W_{t-1} - \ldots$ is non-linear in $W$ because $\nabla_W \mathcal{L}$ passes through the deep net $f$.

CHUNKWISE PARALLEL TRAINING (Sec. 2.2). Define $\xi(i,j) := i - (i \bmod j)$, the start index of the chunk of size $j$ containing position $i$. With chunk size $C$:

Chunkwise Compression: $W_t \leftarrow W_{\xi(t,C)} - \sum_{\tau=\xi(t,C)}^{t} \eta_\tau\, \nabla_W \mathcal{L}\big(f(W_{\xi(t,C)}, k_\tau),\, v_\tau\big)$   (Eq. 3)
Chunkwise Retrieval: $o_t = f(W_t, q_t)$   (Eq. 4)

All gradients inside a chunk are taken at the FROZEN chunk-start state $W_{\xi(t,C)}$ (a first-order / mini-batch-GD approximation of the token-serial recursion), so the per-token gradients are independent given the chunk-start state and can be computed as one batched forward/backward; the per-token states $W_t$ are then a cumulative sum of those gradients. The only remaining serial dependency is across chunks: $W_{nC}$ seeds chunk $n{+}1$. Rationale: this is what makes deep-memory training tractable at all, and it is why chunk size trades quality (gradient staleness within a chunk) against throughput (matmul size).

TNT STAGE 1 -- HIERARCHICAL MEMORY (Sec. 4.1.1). One GLOBAL memory with state $V$ runs the standard sequential chunkwise recursion at a very large chunk $C_G$ (2048+ in experiments):

$V_{(n+1)C_G} \leftarrow V_{nC_G} - \sum_{t=nC_G}^{(n+1)C_G} \eta_t\, \nabla_V \mathcal{L}\big(f(V_{nC_G}, k_t),\, v_t\big), \quad n \in \{0,\ldots,L/\!/C_G\}$   (Eq. 5)

(The printed Eq. 5 mixes indices $n$ and $k$; Appendix E Eq. 13 writes it consistently with a single chunk index.) $V$ carries state over the whole sequence, so long-range context survives; and because $C_G$ is huge, its updates are few, large, compute-dense matmuls that saturate hardware.

N LOCAL memories $W^{(i)}$, $i=1..N$, each with its own chunk size $C_{L_i}$, shard length $S_{L_i}$, and LEARNABLE initial state $W^{(i)}_{init}$, run in parallel with a PERIODIC STATE RESET (base case $N=1$, Eq. 6; general Eq. 14):

$W_t \leftarrow \begin{cases} W_{init} & \text{if } t \equiv 0 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ S_L) \\ W_{t-1} - \sum_{\tau=\xi(t,C_L)}^{t} \eta_\tau\, \nabla_W \mathcal{L}\big(f(W_{\xi(t,C_L)}, k_\tau),\, v_\tau\big) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$   (Eq. 6)

(Faithfulness caveat: the paper prints the base state as $W_{t-1}$ while the gradient anchor is $W_{\xi(t,C_L)}$; taken literally at every $t$ this double-counts intra-chunk gradients relative to Eq. 3's $W_{\xi(t,C)}$ base. Read it as the same chunkwise semantics as Eq. 3 -- chunk-start state minus the cumulative gradient sum up to $t$, gradients anchored at the chunk-start state -- which is the only reading consistent with Eq. 3 and with the described implementation; likely a notational slip.)

The reset is THE key mechanism: every $S_L$ tokens (2048-4096 in experiments), the local state is thrown away and re-initialized to the shared learned $W_{init}$. Consequently shard $m$'s local computation depends on nothing before position $mS_L$: all $L/S_L$ shards can run concurrently -- across devices (context parallelism) or stacked into the batch dimension of one accelerator. This is how TNT parallelizes a NON-linear recurrence over sequence length, something parallel scans cannot do. The price -- local memories lose global context -- is exactly what the global memory pays for. $W_{init}$ being learned (an outer-loop parameter) means every shard starts from a meta-learned prior rather than zeros. The local system can itself be multi-resolution: e.g., $C_L = \{4,8,16,32\}$ means four local modules with different chunk sizes capturing different temporal scales.

TNT STAGE 1 -- Q-K PROJECTION RETRIEVAL (Sec. 4.1.2, App. B, C). Compression fits $f(W,\cdot)$ on the KEY domain; querying with $q_t$ leaves that domain (Challenge 2). TNT projects the query onto the span of the keys seen since the relevant reset/chunk boundary before feeding the LOCAL memory (the global memory gets the raw query -- the fine-grained local memory is judged more sensitive to the mismatch):

$o_t = f\big(V_{\xi(t,C_G)},\, q_t\big) + f\Big(W_t,\ \sum_{\tau=\xi(t,C_L)}^{t} \frac{k_\tau k_\tau^\top}{\|k_\tau\|^2}\, q_t\Big)$   (Eq. 7)

The $N$-local generalization (Eq. 15) sums $f\big(W_t^{(i)}, \sum_{\tau=\xi(t,C_{L_i})}^{t} \frac{k_\tau k_\tau^\top}{\|k_\tau\|^2} q_t\big)$ over $i=1..N$. Note the retrieval uses the GLOBAL state frozen at its chunk start, $V_{\xi(t,C_G)}$, so within a global chunk retrieval reads a stale-but-fixed global memory (this is what makes global retrieval chunk-parallel too). No key cache is needed: the projection matrix $\mathcal{M}_t = \sum_\tau k_\tau k_\tau^\top / \|k_\tau\|^2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ is a constant-size running sum (with L2-normalized keys, common in these models, the denominator drops). Appendix C gives its recurrence with the same reset discipline as the local memory: $\mathcal{M}_t = k_t k_t^\top$ if $t \equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ S_L)$, else $\mathcal{M}_{t-1} + k_t k_t^\top$; and its chunkwise-parallel form $\mathcal{M}_t = \mathcal{M}_{\xi(t,C_L)-1} + \sum_{\tau=\xi(t,C_L)}^{t} k_\tau k_\tau^\top$ (carry-over state plus an intra-chunk prefix scan over outer products); local retrieval is then $f(W_t, \mathcal{M}_t q_t)$. Appendix B shows $\mathcal{M}_t q_t$ is itself a forward pass through an auxiliary LINEAR memory $\mathcal{M}'_t = \mathcal{M}'_{t-1} + k_t k_t^\top$, connecting Q-K Projection to the two-pass read of memory-bounded Transformers (ABC, Gated Slot Attention, Trellis): $W_t = W_{t-1} + \varphi_t v_t^\top$, $o_t = W_t\, \mathrm{softmax}\big(\sum_\tau \varphi_\tau \varphi_\tau^\top q_t\big)$ -- but unlike ABC, TNT's projection applies to deep as well as linear memories, ties the projection features to $k_t$ (no separate $\varphi$ to learn), and sums only from the last reset.

TNT STAGE 2 -- FINE-TUNING AT FINER RESOLUTION (Sec. 4.2). After efficient large-chunk pre-training, continue training briefly with a smaller local chunk size $C_L' < C_L$ (the global $C_G$ stays put). Empirically this not only recovers but SURPASSES the pre-trained quality, at ~5% of pre-training compute (Table 4: 0.15-0.46 hrs vs 3.06-5.55 hrs). The ideal target is $C_L' = 1$, which matches the prefill-and-decode serving pattern: global memory absorbs the prompt in big parallel chunks (prefill), the local memory then updates token-by-token during generation (decode). Design rationale for the whole two-stage split: chunk size is no longer one compromise value -- it is a TRAINING-throughput knob in Stage 1 and an INFERENCE-resolution knob in Stage 2.

WHY EACH PIECE EXISTS, in one line each: large-$C_G$ global memory = hardware saturation + long-range context; reset-to-$W_{init}$ locals = the only known way to context-parallelize a non-linear deep-memory recurrence; learnable $W_{init}$ = meta-learned shard prior; multi-resolution $\{C_{L_i}\}$ = multi-scale temporal features; Q-K projection = closes the key-write/query-read domain gap with $O(d^2)$ state; global-side raw query = mismatch matters less at coarse granularity, saves compute; Stage 2 = cures chunk-size over-specialization for pennies and unlocks chunk-1 decode.
outer_loop_training:
WHAT IS META-LEARNED (slow weights $\theta$, trained by AdamW on next-token cross-entropy): the q/k/v projection matrices feeding every memory module, the data-dependent inner learning-rate maps producing $\eta_t$, the FeedForward block after the memory layer (Fig. 3), the shared learnable local initial states $W^{(i)}_{init}$ (one per local module -- these are genuine outer-loop parameters that define where every shard's inner loop starts), and the usual embeddings/head. Outer optimizer: AdamW, weight decay 0.1, cosine schedule, peak LR 1e-3, T5 tokenizer (32k vocab), 150M params, 10B tokens, TPUv5 pod (2x2x2 topology, model parallelism 2), implemented in plain JAX with no custom kernels.

HOW GRADIENTS FLOW THROUGH THE INNER LOOP (scaffolding for training-naive readers): the fast-weight states $W_t, V_t$ are not parameters -- they are ACTIVATIONS of the outer computation graph, produced by the symbolic gradient-descent expressions in Eqs. 5-6. Backprop therefore differentiates THROUGH those inner GD steps: the outer gradient of the LM loss w.r.t. $\theta$ includes second-order terms $\partial(\nabla_W \mathcal{L})/\partial\theta$ flowing through every inner update. Chunkwise anchoring is what keeps this tractable: within a chunk all inner gradients are functions of one frozen state, so the whole chunk is a single batched forward+backward through $f$, and the backprop graph's SERIAL depth equals the number of chunk-boundary handoffs, not the number of tokens.

WHAT TNT CHANGES ABOUT THAT GRAPH: (a) For local memories, the reset to $W_{init}$ cuts the graph every $S_L$ tokens -- there is NO gradient path across shard boundaries through local states, so the serial chain per shard is only $S_L/C_L$ chunk handoffs and the $L/S_L$ shards are fully independent (parallel across devices, or folded into the batch axis). $W_{init}$ receives gradient from every shard, giving it a dense, well-averaged learning signal. (b) For the global memory, the chain is $L/C_G$ handoffs (e.g., 16k/2048 = 8 sequential steps per sequence) -- short enough that its serial recurrence is cheap even though it is non-linear. (c) The Q-K projection matrix $\mathcal{M}_t$ is computed by a parallel prefix scan of $k_\tau k_\tau^\top$ within chunks plus a $d\times d$ carry between chunks, reset at shard boundaries, so it adds no serial bottleneck.

TWO-STAGE SCHEDULE: Stage 1 does the bulk of pre-training at large local chunks (experiments: $C_L \in \{8\}$ up to $\{4,8,16,32\}$ with $S_L$ = 2048-4096, $C_G$ = 2048). Stage 2 continues training the SAME objective for a small number of steps with the local chunk size reduced to $C_L' < C_L$ (evaluated down to $\{1\}$), costing ~5% of Stage 1 compute (Table 4: 0.15-0.46 hrs on top of 3.06-5.55 hrs). The abstract phrases this as 'only the local memory modules are adapted to a smaller chunksize'; Sec. 4.2 says 'we continue training the efficiently pre-trained model with a smaller local chunk size' -- the unambiguous part is that only the LOCAL chunk-size hyperparameter changes (global stays at $C_G$); whether any slow weights are frozen during Stage 2 is not spelled out, and the natural reading of Sec. 4.2 is that training simply continues end-to-end at the new resolution.
inner_loop_test_time:
STATE THAT EVOLVES DURING INFERENCE (per memory layer): the global fast weights $V$ (a deep sub-network's parameters), $N$ local fast weights $W^{(i)}$ (each a deep sub-network's parameters), and $N$ Q-K projection matrices $\mathcal{M}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$. All are constant-size in sequence length. The learned $W^{(i)}_{init}$ and slow weights are frozen.

UPDATE RULES AT INFERENCE (identical in form to training -- that is the point of test-time memorization): (1) Global: once every $C_G$ tokens, $V \mathrel{-}= \sum_{t \in \text{chunk}} \eta_t \nabla_V \mathcal{L}(f(V,k_t),v_t)$ with all gradients at the chunk-start $V$ -- one big batched forward+backward over $C_G$ tokens; between updates, retrieval reads the frozen chunk-start $V$. (2) Local $i$: every $C_{L_i}'$ tokens, the anchored cumulative GD update of Eq. 6; after Stage 2 fine-tuning at $C_L'=1$ this is EXACT per-token online gradient descent, $W_t = W_{t-1} - \eta_t \nabla_W \mathcal{L}(f(W_{t-1},k_t),v_t)$, and every $S_{L_i}$ tokens the state is reset to $W^{(i)}_{init}$ (and $\mathcal{M}^{(i)}$ to $k_t k_t^\top$). The inner optimizer in this paper's instantiation is PLAIN gradient descent with learned per-token step size $\eta_t$ -- deliberately simplified; Appendix D notes Titans-style momentum+forget gating, Comba-style closed-loop objectives, or Adam/Muon inner optimizers are all compatible but unexplored here. (3) Projection: $\mathcal{M}_t = \mathcal{M}_{t-1} + k_t k_t^\top$ (rank-1, $O(d^2)$), with shard resets.

PER-TOKEN COST (decode, $C_L'=1$): let $P_f$ = parameter count of one memory sub-network $f$ (for a 2-layer MLP with hidden width $h$: $P_f \approx 2dh$). Each local module costs one forward+backward through $f$ for compression (~$3 \times 2P_f$ FLOPs, i.e., ~$6P_f$) plus one forward for retrieval (~$2P_f$), plus $2d^2$ for the rank-1 $\mathcal{M}$ update and $2d^2$ for the mat-vec $\mathcal{M}_t q_t$. The global module amortizes the same per-token gradient work into one dense batch per 2048 tokens (compute-dense, negligible latency impact per token) plus a per-token retrieval forward against the frozen $V$. Total decode state per layer $\approx (1{+}N)\,P_f + N d^2$ numbers, CONSTANT in context length $L$ -- versus a Transformer KV cache of $2 L d$ per layer that grows without bound and must be re-read every step. Crucially, Stage 2 exists precisely so that this $C_L'=1$ decode mode is the QUALITY-OPTIMAL operating point rather than a catastrophic train/test mismatch (Challenge 3 / Figure 2), and the reset mechanism means prefill of the local memories over a long prompt is embarrassingly parallel across $L/S_L$ shards while the global memory prefills in $L/C_G$ large sequential-but-dense steps.

concepts_introduced.name: Deep memory module
concepts_introduced.definition: The paper's umbrella term (imported/formalized from TTT/Titans/Atlas lineage) for a layer whose recurrent state is the parameter vector W of a deep sub-network f(W,.) updated by inner-loop gradient descent; distilled into two per-token ops, Memory Compression (write via GD on a self-supervised loss) and Memory Retrieval (read via forward pass), as opposed to linear memory modules with matrix states and linear transitions.

concepts_introduced.name: xi(i,j) chunk-start function
concepts_introduced.definition: xi(i,j) := i - (i mod j); notational device giving the first index of the size-j chunk containing position i, used throughout the chunkwise equations.

concepts_introduced.name: Challenge 1/2/3 taxonomy
concepts_introduced.definition: The paper's named decomposition of what blocks deep memories: (1) no efficient training implementation (memory-bound small chunks, <5-10% FLOPs utilization), (2) compression/retrieval domain inconsistency (write with keys, read with queries), (3) performance sensitivity to a fixed pre-training chunk size (train/inference chunk mismatch, Figure 2).

concepts_introduced.name: TNT (Titans iNside Titans / TTT iNside TTT)
concepts_introduced.definition: The two-stage training paradigm: efficiency-focused hierarchical pre-training (Stage 1) followed by performance-focused fine-tuning at finer chunk resolution (Stage 2), decoupling training efficiency from inference performance; model-agnostic over deep memory architectures.

concepts_introduced.name: Hierarchical memory (global + N local)
concepts_introduced.definition: One sequential global deep memory V at huge chunk size C_G (2048+) for long-range context, plus N parallel local deep memories W^(i), each with its own chunk size C_L_i, shard length S_L_i, and learnable init W_init^(i); outputs are summed at retrieval.

concepts_introduced.name: Periodic state reset / learnable W_init
concepts_introduced.definition: Local memory states are re-initialized every S_L tokens to a shared OUTER-LOOP-LEARNED initial state W_init, severing all sequential dependency across shards; the paper's key trick for context-parallelizing a NON-linear recurrence (where parallel scans do not apply).

concepts_introduced.name: Context parallelism for non-linear RNNs
concepts_introduced.definition: The resulting capability: the L/S_L independent shards of the local-memory computation can be distributed across devices or stacked on the batch axis of one accelerator, unlike prior deep-memory training whose chunk-to-chunk chain is strictly serial.

concepts_introduced.name: Q-K Projection
concepts_introduced.definition: Retrieval fix for Challenge 2: feed the local memory f(W_t, M_t q_t) where M_t = sum_tau k_tau k_tau^T / ||k_tau||^2 is a running key-outer-product (projection onto the observed-key subspace), maintained as a constant d x d state via chunkwise prefix scan with shard resets; global memory keeps the raw query. Appendix B links it to the two-pass read of memory-bounded Transformers (ABC/GSA/Trellis) with tied features and reset-scoped sums.

concepts_introduced.name: Chunk-size mismatch (train/test chunk sensitivity)
concepts_introduced.definition: New empirical finding (Figure 2): a deep memory pre-trained at chunk C is only optimal when INFERRED at chunk C (550M Titans at C=64: ppl 13.78 at 64 vs 36.45 at 8 and 22.4 at 512), contradicting the fresher-is-better intuition and motivating Stage 2.

concepts_introduced.name: Stage 2 fine-tuning at finer resolution
concepts_introduced.definition: Brief continued training with local chunk size C_L' < C_L (down to 1) at ~5% of pre-training compute, which recovers and surpasses pre-trained quality and specializes the model for chunk-1 decoding.

concepts_introduced.name: Multi-resolution local memory set C_L = {...}
concepts_introduced.definition: Configuration notation and design: multiple local modules with different chunk sizes (e.g., {4,8,16,32}) capturing multi-scale temporal dynamics; each added resolution monotonically improved perplexity in the ablation.

concepts_introduced.name: Prefill/decode alignment of the hierarchy
concepts_introduced.definition: The serving-facing interpretation: global memory (large chunks, compute-dense) handles context prefill; the Stage-2-adapted local memory (chunk 1) handles iterative decoding.

assumptions_and_scope:
Scale and setup: all quality results are 150M-parameter models trained on 10B tokens with a T5 32k tokenizer on a TPUv5 pod (2x2x2, model parallelism 2), in JAX WITHOUT custom kernels; the chunk-sensitivity study (Fig. 2) uses a 550M Titans. Efficiency runs: context 2k-32k, 0.5M-token batches, S_L=2048; quality runs: 16k context, 1M-token batches, S_L=4096, C_G=2048. TTT and Titans baselines are the authors' own re-implementations (footnote 2), trained in the same setup.

Instantiation simplifications (important): although marketed on Titans, the studied memory module 'optimizes its inner-loop with gradient descent' only -- Appendix D concedes that Titans' momentum and forget gating, Mamba2-style gating, Comba closed-loop objectives, and Adam/Muon inner optimizers were all left out for clarity. So TNT is validated on a SIMPLIFIED Titans/TTT hybrid; transfer of the 17x speedup and quality gains to fully-gated Titans or Atlas is asserted as applicable but not measured. TNT is a training paradigm, not an architecture: its claims are about throughput and chunk-size decoupling, not about beating Transformers -- the Gated Transformer still wins perplexity (22.39 vs 23.09) and FlashAttention still wins raw step time except at 32K.

Scaffolding flags for the inference-audience write-up: (1) chunkwise INNER-loop training and why gradient 'anchoring' at chunk starts is an approximation, (2) backprop-through-gradient-descent (fast weights as activations, second-order terms) -- needed to understand what 'learnable W_init' and 'learned eta_t' mean, (3) context parallelism vs tensor/pipeline parallelism, (4) time-to-target-loss as the efficiency metric in Table 1 (vs per-step time in Fig. 4), (5) why small-chunk training is memory-bound (many small ops, poor arithmetic intensity). Notation caveats to preserve: Eq. 5's n/k index mixing (App. E Eq. 13 is the clean form) and Eq. 6's printed base state W_{t-1} where chunkwise semantics (Eq. 3) requires the chunk-start state W_{xi(t,C_L)} as the base of the cumulative sum.
experiments_and_scale:
All at 150M params / 10B tokens unless noted. SPEED (Fig. 4/5, per-step runtime, 0.5M tokens/batch, 2k-32k context): TNT scales linearly with sequence length; Titans and JAX attention scale quadratically in wall-clock. At 32K: TNT is 5.1x faster than Titans at the same memory chunk (C_L=C=16), and TNT with C_L={128} in plain JAX is 1.3x faster than the FlashAttention (Pallas) kernel. TIME-TO-QUALITY (Table 1, hours to reach training loss 3.20): Titans C=8 19.48h (1.00x), C=16 10.79h, C=32 6.45h, C=64 4.18h, C=128 3.71h; TNT {8} 2.54h (7.68x), {16} 1.65h (11.78x), {32} 1.22h (15.92x), {64} 1.12h (17.37x, the headline), {128} 1.16h (16.75x); Transformers: JAX w/o gating 1.74h, w/ gating 1.38h, FlashAttention w/o gating 1.23h, w/ gating 0.96h (20.22x) -- so TNT matches vanilla-JAX Transformers but not kernel-optimized Gated Transformer (no custom TNT kernel yet). Same-chunk comparison isolates the architecture: at chunk 8, TNT is 7.7x faster than Titans.

QUALITY (Table 2; C4/FineWeb/PG19 ppl + PIQA/HellaSwag/ARC-e/CSQA acc; C_G=2048): Transformer 23.58 avg ppl / 38.3 avg acc; Gated Transformer 22.39 / 39.7; TTT (C=256) 27.62 / 38.1; Titans (C=256) 27.13 / 38.8; Titans (C=8) 25.07 / 39.0. TNT Stage 1: {8} 24.10, {8,16} 23.80, {4,8,16} 23.44, {4,8,16,32} 23.13 avg ppl (accs ~40.2-41.0). TNT Stage 2 (on the corresponding Stage 1 models, chunk sets {1},{2,4},{2,4,8},{2,4,8,16}): 23.99, 23.77, 23.36, 23.09 avg ppl (accs ~40.3-40.9). So best TNT beats all RNN baselines and the vanilla Transformer on ppl, beats even Gated Transformer on reasoning acc (41.0 vs 39.7), loses to Gated Transformer on ppl. TRAINING COST (Table 4): Titans C=8 8.44h vs TNT Stage 1 {8} 3.06h ... {4,8,16,32} 5.55h; Stage 2 adds only 0.15-0.46h (~5%). ABLATIONS (Table 3, ppl/acc): Titans base 23.53/38.8; +1..4 local memories 21.04/40.6 -> 20.74/41.0 -> 20.47/40.2 -> 20.15/40.6 (monotone ppl gains); REMOVING global memory: 25.60/35.5 (worse than base -- resets without global context are fatal); removing Q-K projection: 22.01/36.4 (vs 21.04 -- projection is worth ~1 ppl); +Stage 2 on N=1: 20.86/40.9. CHUNK SENSITIVITY (Fig. 2, 550M Titans pre-trained C=64): inference ppl 36.45/34.15/24.23/13.78/15.5/17.88/22.4 at C=8/16/32/64/128/256/512.
systems_implications:
PARALLELIZATION STRUCTURE. TNT converts the worst-parallelizing sequence layer known (a non-linear deep-net-valued recurrence) into three well-behaved pieces: (a) a global recurrence with only L/C_G sequential handoffs per sequence (8 at 16k context with C_G=2048), each handoff a huge batched matmul over 2048 tokens -- compute-bound by construction; (b) L/S_L fully independent local shards -- true context parallelism: shard across devices with zero cross-device state exchange for the local path, or stack shards on the batch axis of one accelerator to fatten every kernel launch; (c) a d x d prefix-scan for the Q-K projection with a single d x d carry between chunks. This attacks the root cause of the reported <5-10% FLOPs utilization of deep-memory training: it is not FLOPs that are missing but arithmetic intensity, and TNT manufactures intensity by making the parallel work units big (global) or numerous-and-independent (local).

KERNELS. Everything is plain JAX; there is no fused kernel, and the authors explicitly leave one to future work -- yet at 32K context TNT (C_L=128) already beats FlashAttention per step. For the study's audience: linear-attention-style SRAM chunk kernels (GLA/DeltaNet lineage) do NOT port to deep memories because inter-chunk state propagation passes through non-linearities (MLP forward/backward, LayerNorm), so TNT's reset trick is currently the only lever; a fused TNT kernel would fuse the per-chunk batched fwd+bwd of f with the cumulative-sum state updates.

STATE VS KV CACHE. Decode-time state per memory layer is (1+N) P_f + N d^2 (fast weights of global + N locals + N projection matrices), constant in L; a Transformer holds 2 L d per layer and re-reads it every token. At L = 32k+ this is the usual RNN memory-bandwidth argument, but TNT adds two serving-specific wins: (1) Stage 2 makes chunk-1 decoding the accuracy-OPTIMAL mode, aligning quality with the natural autoregressive loop instead of fighting it (Challenge 3 showed baseline deep memories lose ~2.6x ppl when decoded at chunk 8 after training at 64); (2) prefill maps cleanly onto hardware -- the global memory ingests the prompt in C_G-sized dense batches while local shards prefill in parallel, so time-to-first-token scales like a chunked linear pass, not a serial recurrence. The periodic reset also bounds how much local state history a preemption/restore must reconstruct (at most S_L tokens per local module, given the shard-start states are a constant W_init).

THROUGHPUT CHARACTER. Wall-clock is linear in L at fixed token budget (Fig. 4); the crossover vs quadratic attention appears within 2k-32k. Larger C_L monotonically buys speed until ~{64}-{128} where time-to-quality bottoms out (Table 1: 1.12h at {64}, 1.16h at {128}) -- past that, quality loss per step outweighs step-time gains. Training-cost accounting must include Stage 2, but it is noise (~5%). Caveat for capacity planning: multi-resolution configs multiply memory-module compute -- Stage 1 training time grows from 3.06h ({8}) to 5.55h ({4,8,16,32}) -- and decode cost likewise scales with N; the quality-vs-N trade (Table 3) is roughly -0.3 ppl per added module at this scale.
connections: LINEAGE BACKWARD, within the study set: TNT's base model and main baseline is Titans (2501.00663) -- it inherits Titans' deep-memory-with-inner-GD formulation but strips momentum and forget gating for clarity (App. D), and its 'Titans iNside Titans' hierarchy of memories at different timescales is a training-driven answer to the same multi-timescale instinct Titans expressed via persistent + long-term + short-term memory. It cites and positions against the conceptual frame of 2504.13173 (It's All Connected / Miras: memory = online optimization of an attentional-bias objective; TNT's Challenge 2 and Q-K projection are a surgical fix INSIDE that frame -- change the retrieval input domain rather than the objective) and against Atlas (2505.23735), whose Omega-rule sliding-window updates and Muon inner optimizer are named in App. D as compatible future combinations; Atlas also shares authors. Relative to the later papers in the set (2512.24695, 2606.03979), TNT is upstream infrastructure: whatever architectural sophistication later entries add, they inherit the chunkwise-training economics TNT diagnoses, and TNT's reset-based context parallelism and two-resolution (train big / serve small) recipe are the kind of substrate those designs would train on. EXTERNAL LINEAGE: TTT / Sun et al. 2024 (the other explicit target model; TNT's Challenge 1 quotes its 16-64 token chunks); fast weight programmers (Schmidhuber 1992/93, Schlag et al. 2021) as the ancestral write-by-outer-product memory; the delta-rule line DeltaNet -> Gated DeltaNet -> DeltaProduct and Longhorn/RWKV-7 as the LINEAR-memory competitors whose chunkwise kernels TNT cannot reuse (non-linear states) but whose throughput it chases; Mamba/Mamba2 gating as a pluggable extension; LaCT ('Test-time training done right', Zhang, Bi, et al. 2025) as the closest prior -- large chunks + window attention -- criticized for mixing attention back in and ignoring chunk-1 decode; log-linear attention (Guo et al. 2025) as the hierarchical-memory prior restricted to linear modules; ABC / Gated Slot Attention / Trellis as the two-pass memory-bounded Transformers that Appendix B reveals as Q-K Projection's relatives; Hopfield-network associative-memory theory as the deep background (App. A). WHAT IT LEAVES OPEN: it does not close the quality gap to Gated Transformers (22.39 vs 23.09 ppl) and says so; it validates only plain-GD inner loops (no momentum/gating/Muon/Comba feedback -- all deferred); no custom kernel; no scaling study beyond 150M (550M only for the sensitivity plot); and the reset mechanism's interaction with tasks requiring exact recall across shard boundaries (needle-in-haystack style) is not evaluated -- everything rests on the global memory catching what the resets drop.
open_questions: (1) Scale: does the 'TNT beats its own baseline while training 17x faster' result hold at 1B+ params and 100B+ tokens, where Titans-class models are usually claimed to shine? Only 150M is trained; the chunk-sensitivity phenomenon itself was shown at 550M. (2) Recall under resets: local memories forget everything every S_L tokens by design; no associative-recall / needle benchmarks are reported, so how much long-range retrieval really survives via the C_G=2048 global memory (whose retrieval reads a chunk-start-frozen, hence up-to-2048-tokens-stale, state) is unmeasured. (3) Full Titans/Atlas instantiation: App. D defers momentum, forget gating, Comba closed loops, and Adam/Muon inner optimizers -- do resets and Q-K projection compose with gated/momentum updates, and does Stage 2 still transfer? (4) Stage 2 mechanics: what exactly is trained (all weights vs local-memory-adjacent ones), how many steps are needed, and is there a curriculum over chunk sizes (they fine-tune {4,8,16,32} -> {2,4,8,16} and {8} -> {1}, suggesting halving)? Why does fine-tuning {1} on {8}-pretrained give 23.99 while {2,4,8,16} on {4,8,16,32} gives 23.09 -- is chunk-1-everywhere ever optimal for multi-module configs? (5) Kernels: how far does a fused chunk-parallel kernel for deep-memory fwd+bwd close the remaining gap to FlashAttention Gated Transformers (0.96h vs 1.12h time-to-loss)? (6) Hyperparameter geometry: how to choose S_L vs C_G vs the resolution set {C_L_i} jointly (experiments only probe S_L in {2048,4096}, C_G=2048); does the optimal hierarchy deepen with context length? (7) Theory: no analysis of what the reset costs in expressivity (e.g., state-tracking arguments a la Merrill et al.) or of why chunk-size over-specialization (Fig. 2) happens; both are empirical observations awaiting explanation. (8) Serving: quantitative decode throughput/latency and memory numbers for the chunk-1 mode vs a KV-cache Transformer are not reported -- the prefill/decode story is architectural, not benchmarked.
